coreStoryFacts.text: Chainlink will connect bank systems and signing infrastructure to Swift’s blockchain ledger through its platform.
Chainlink did not provide a timetable for individual banks to adopt its connection framework or identify which of Swift’s pilot banks will use CRE first.
Sergey Nazarov, CEO of Chainlink Labs, said the company was “thrilled to be supporting the Swift ledger” as banks seek technology for tokenized deposits and ledger connectivity.
The latest work extends a relationship between Chainlink and Swift that has covered institutional blockchain interoperability for several years.
Swift has stressed that the blockchain ledger does not replace its role as a global financial messaging network.
As crypto.news previously reported, Swift’s first ledger deployment uses tokenized deposits issued by banks instead of a public cryptocurrency bridge asset.
Swift’s ledger supports 24/7 tokenized deposit payments while final settlement continues through existing agreed mechanisms.
Swift says its network connects more than 11,500 institutions and corporates across over 200 markets.
Swift disclosed in March that the ledger’s first iteration uses an Ethereum Virtual Machine-compatible architecture based on Hyperledger Besu, an open-source enterprise blockchain platform.
Swift operates the ledger and coordinates interbank processes, including validation of funding commitments.
CRE lets institutions retain transaction signing keys while orchestrating workflows that access Swift’s shared ledger.
The deposits remain on bank-owned ledgers, while Swift coordinates payment commitments between participating institutions before final settlement.

Previous work examined how financial institutions could use existing Swift infrastructure alongside blockchain networks, including experiments involving tokenized assets and cross-chain communication.
Swift itself remains the operator of the new ledger.
Chainlink describes CRE as the workflow layer responsible for coordinating interactions while each bank signs its own transactions.
Chainlink repeated the same distinction in its Sept.
Chainlink is working to enable financial institutions in Swift's community to read and write to Swift's blockchain ledger through its platform.
The integration supports tokenized deposits and 24/7 cross-border payments, with CRE orchestrating workflows under each institution's key control.

BNY, Citi, and Wells Fargo represent North America. From Europe, BNP Paribas, HSBC, Lloyds Bank, Standard Chartered, and UBS anchor the group. ANZ, DBS, MUFG Bank, OCBC, and UOB cover Australia, Singapore, Japan, and the broader Asia Pacific footprint. First Abu Dhabi Bank and Mashreq bring UAE representation. Itaú Unibanco covers Brazil, and FirstRand Bank rounds out the roster from Africa.

The ledger supports 24/7 movement of tokenized deposits, including overnight and weekend transfers. Banks then complete final settlement through existing systems. Thierry Chilosi, SWIFT’s Chief Business Officer, said the capability extends the trust of established finance into digital money. SWIFT built the ledger in nine months with input from international financial institutions.

Every two to three days, SWIFT messages move value equal to global GDP. Historically, the network handled instructions rather than settlement. The two networks have collaborated since 2023. Their early pilots proved that SWIFT messages could trigger tokenized asset transfers across public and private chains. UBS, BNY, BNP Paribas, Citi, ANZ, and Lloyds all took part in that work.

UBS became the first global asset manager to adopt it. The standard lets institutions manage tokenized fund workflows from existing systems using SWIFT messages formatted in ISO 20022.

A separate corporate actions initiative launched at the same event. It includes SWIFT, DTCC, Euroclear, Wellington Management, and more than 20 additional institutions. The Chainlink Runtime Environment orchestrates the workflow. CCIP then distributes confirmed records to DTCC’s blockchain ecosystem and other chains.

In November 2025, SWIFT moved the Chainlink integration from pilot to production. Member banks can now route tokenized asset instructions through CCIP using ISO 20022 messages. They can attach blockchain wallet addresses directly to payment instructions. They can also settle tokenized currencies, bonds, and equities across banking and blockchain networks in the same message flow.

ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE (AP) — Pope Leo XIV said Monday that concerns about artificial intelligence going rogue are not "fake news" and should be taken seriously, insisting that safety issues raised by AI experts should be discussed and acted on. Leo, who dedicated his first encyclical to AI and protecting humanity in its wake, was asked during a press conference about what the United States and China especially should be doing to prevent AI from posing catastrophic risks to humanity. President Donald Trump has called concerns about AI going rogue a "hoax." Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "This is a problem that I think we need to sit down and talk about," the American pope told reporters returning home from France. "We can't just sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen." Trump has been a champion of AI , often warning that the United States must remain ahead of China in the technological arms race. He has said efforts to limit the technology were part of a "conspiracy" by his political opponents. Several AI giants, including Anthropic, have called for a slowdown in development to give safety measures time to catch up to the fast-moving technology. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for example, has warned that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet. Trump said on Sunday he planned to have a late dinner with Amodei, but he has not yet commented on the meeting. "If someone were to ask me 'Am I in panic mode?' No I'm not. I sleep at night," Leo said. "I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI should be taken seriously." "I don't think that that is 'fake news' as some have said to try and cause whether financial or other some other kind of benefit," Leo said. The pope, who called for robust AI regulation and a slowdown in the technology in his first encyclical "Magnificent Humanity," is up to speed on developments. Despite being at the end of a grueling four-day trip to France , Leo noted a news report Monday afternoon about Nvidia introducing guardrails into AI. He also noted that the company has previously resisted outside regulation of AI development. "We need to continue to invite political leaders, leaders of AI, social organizations, associations to come together and look at what is happening already and what could be down the road," he said. "To simply say 'Oh it's not going to happen' and close our eyes to it I think is probably not the most responsible way to go about that," he added. The warning comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry and reports continue to emerge about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also go rogue and carry out other, more harmful tasks. The worries have grown so loud that the CEO of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said in an interview with Fortune that his company would wait until next year to start selling its stock to investors on Wall Street as it focuses on safety. Leo noted that ever since he published his encyclical in May, the Vatican has received comments from people interested in being part of a broader conversation about AI. A Vatican commission is working to promote dialogue, study and investigation "to find ways to make sure that AI does not get to a point of destroying humanity or removing humanity from the conversation," he said. Leo said he was "relatively optimistic" that solutions could be found. "I think there are enough people seriously interested in that and willing to look at that outside of the questions once again of power, who gets there first," he said. Leo had identified AI as one of t he biggest challenges to humanity within days of his election. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform designed to stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue , saying it sets “boundaries” that could have stopped previous breaches. The announcement of the company's Open Agent Safety Platform follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations. The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control. Nvidia executives said in a media briefing the new, open-source system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face . “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI. The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed the safety concerns about AI, which was followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI's models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own. Earlence Fernandes, an associate professor at the University of California, San Diego's computer science and engineering department, called Nvidia's security platform a “step in the right direction.” “We need more work that seeks to build protections around the model. I’ve been talking about how traditional cybersecurity ideas are necessary to help control and secure AI agents for a while now," he said in an email. “There are however, several challenges that traditional cyber security approaches still cannot currently solve. For example, what is a good security policy to configure the system with? An agent needs access to real resources to be useful, but giving it the minimum amount of access is tricky and non-trivial.” Fernandes added that to solve the AI security problem, both sides need to cooperate, with companies continuing to invest in alignment efforts and the open source community and academia "creating systems-level solutions to account for when a model does engage in unwanted behavior.” Nvidia, based in Santa Clara, California, makes high-end chips that have emerged as the leading building blocks for AI. The company's board has cleared the way for the company to spend $150 billion more in share buybacks , bringing its stock repurchase program to $235 billion, the company said Monday. Nvidia's security software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said. Because it's open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel. The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard chips to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can "intervene instantly" if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said. “OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” he said. Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase. The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. But others including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address. coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform designed to stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue , saying it sets “boundaries” that could have stopped previous breaches.
The Open Agent Safety Platform includes software that sets boundaries for AI agents.
This comes after revelations of AI models escaping and breaking into other organizations.
Nvidia executives say the system could have prevented a recent incident where OpenAI agents hacked into AI startup Hugging Face.
Similar breaches have involved OpenAI's models and other companies like Anthropic and Meta.
Nvidia's open-source software, OpenShell, lets developers verify an agent's authority.
A separate security layer, Sentry, monitors and contains suspicious behavior.
Over 100 companies are already using the system.
Earlence Fernandes, an associate professor at the University of California, San Diego's computer science and engineering department, called Nvidia's security platform a “step in the right direction.”
Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase.
Nvidia, based in Santa Clara, California, makes high-end chips that have emerged as the leading building blocks for AI.
The company's board has cleared the way for the company to spend $150 billion more in share buybacks , bringing its stock repurchase program to $235 billion, the company said Monday.
FILE - A logo of Nvidia is displayed at at the Computex Taipei exhibition, one of the world's largest computer and technology expos, in Taipei, Taiwan, Wednesday, June 3, 2026.

Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.

The Federal Aviation Administration ( FAA ) is currently assessing whether this poses a wider safety issue, which means another setback for the American plane maker.

Boeing had hoped that the MAX 10 would receive certification for the largest type of the MAX family of planes this month . The plane maker's Chief Executive Officer, Kelly Ortberg, had told investors earlier this month that Boeing had hoped for the 'green light' on the variant very soon.

To date, the administration has yet to determine whether the software issue affects the safety of flight and, as a result, is going to delay the certification of the MAX 10 until the agency is satisfied that there is not a wider issue. Bryan Bedford , the FAA Administrator, confirmed this at a press conference in Washington, D.C., on Monday, as reported by CNBC .
Safety will continue to dictate the certification timeline for the MAX 10; the agency confirmed the process will take as much time as required to investigate the software glitch.
Following these comments from Bedford, Boeing's shares dropped around 7%, as the American plane maker faces another delay on what has been a tumultuous journey for the aircraft.

Over the past weekend, details came to light that Boeing had known for two years about a potential software issue on select MAX aircraft. This is where the vertical navigation system may interfere when an aircraft misses an approach and is forced to complete a go-around. This is a common occurrence when there are runway incursions. While pilots are trained to operate the aircraft without this software, the concern is now focused on whether this would maintain a suitable workload for the crew.

Pilots will remain in control of the aircraft during all types of scenarios, and it only affects the U.14 version of the software . The MAX 7 , which was certified last month, is the latest type of aircraft that has the software, which the FAA is closely investigating. Boeing is working with carriers Southwest and United to work through any other concerns.
Bedford confirmed that Boeing had fixed previous bugs in the system; however the new issue will require airlines with the newer software to revert to older software until the issue is resolved.

Both of these crashes involved the flight control systems of these aircraft and, as a result, forced the global grounding of the type while the root causes were investigated .

sources.title: FAA Reviews 737 MAX Flight-Guidance Software Issue as Boeing Seeks 737-10 Certification - Airways Magazine
passages: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft.
Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10.
Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported.

In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem.
The FAA's statement did not address either program.
Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps."

Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review.

Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September .
Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more .
In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year.
He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months."
CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward.
The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers.
CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment.
Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes."

In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week .
Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue.

CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach.

In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively. Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem. CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week . VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach. Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward. The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported. The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them. An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update. The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version. The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September . Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps." Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months." The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution. Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. The FAA's statement to Airways did not say whether the CARB must conclude before the agency certifies the 737-10. Copyright © 2026 Airways Publishing LLC. All rights reserved. ‍

coreStoryFacts.text: The head of the Federal Aviation Administration said a software problem will delay its certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10 as the agency assesses whether it poses a safety issue, a potential setback for the manufacturer as it seeks to complete government approval of its best-selling family of aircraft.
Boeing had expected to receive a green light from its regulator on the years-delayed planes "very soon," CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors earlier this month.
"We continue to follow the lead of the FAA as we work through the certification process," Boeing said in a statement.
The company had originally planned to start delivering the Max 10 in 2020 before those safety concerns and other problems delayed the plane.
It is the last of the Max family waiting to be certified.
A flight control system was implicated in those crashes.

"We haven't concluded whether this is a safety-of-flight issue or not, but we will be delaying the 10 ... until we're satisfied that we don't have an issue here," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference on air traffic modernization in Washington, D.C., on Monday.
Boeing shares extended earlier losses after Bedford's comments, shedding nearly 7% Monday, as investors assessed another delay after years of setbacks for the aircraft.
It isn't clear how that could affect deliveries of those planes to customers like Southwest Airlines .

Boeing said over the weekend that the issue could occur with a vertical navigation system after an aircraft misses an approach and has to go around and line up to land again, such as in situations when there is an obstruction on the runway, for example.
Both the company and Bedford said pilots are trained for those circumstances.
Bedford said Boeing had fixed a previous bug in the system but "unexpectedly ... introduced a new bug."
The impending certification of the long-awaited Boeing 737 MAX 10 could be delayed, following the assessment that a potential software problem has come to light.
The Federal Aviation Administration ( FAA ) is currently assessing whether this poses a wider safety issue, which means another setback for the American plane maker.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is reviewing an issue in updated flight management computer (FMC) software on some Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Two U.S. airlines have told Boeing they will not accept new aircraft carrying the software, and the review comes as Boeing awaits certification of the 737-10. In a statement to Airways, the FAA said it is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain 737 MAX aircraft and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines. The agency said it "will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern." According to the FAA, a CARB consists of FAA safety experts and is the agency's standard process for determining whether an issue is a safety concern and, if so, how to address it most effectively. Boeing told operators in a bulletin in late August that the glitch is not an immediate safety issue , CBS reported. In a statement to Airways, a Boeing spokesperson said the company informed all 737 operators last month "about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario" and "shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases." The spokesperson said Boeing's engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue. The Wall Street Journal first reported the problem. CBS reported that the condition can arise in rare cases when the crew is flying a precision approach with the autopilot engaged, initiates a missed approach, or go-around, and then changes the preprogrammed flight plan. In that situation, the flight guidance system may incorrectly transition out of vertical navigation (VNAV) to a simpler pitch mode such as level change or vertical speed, according to Boeing's description of the problem reported by Aviation Week . VNAV follows the vertical profile the FMC computes from the flight plan's altitude and speed constraints. Level change instead holds a target airspeed while the autothrottle sets climb or idle thrust, and vertical speed holds a rate of climb or descent the pilot selects. Neither mode follows the FMC's vertical path, so crews must manage those constraints themselves. CBS noted the scenario would typically occur close to the airport, where crew workload is already high, and Boeing said pilots must take additional steps to use automated guidance on the next approach. Boeing said the autopilot continues to function if VNAV disengages and that pilots are trained to land without it. The company told CNBC it is "working directly with airlines to formalize a procedure that will allow pilots to reenable automated vertical navigation should this situation occur." Boeing told Airways it "anticipates the next software update in 2028" and is working to accelerate that timeline based on operator feedback. CBS reported that Boeing's initial bulletin also said updated pilot guidance would follow in November, and that Boeing is working to bring both forward. The glitch surfaced in FMC software versions 14 and 14.1, CBS reported. Alaska Airlines (AS), American Airlines (AA), Southwest Airlines (WN), and United Airlines (UA) each told CBS that none of their in-service 737 MAX aircraft use the affected software. Southwest told CNBC that "none of our fleet is equipped with Version U.14, including new deliveries of Max 8 airplanes." Those statements concern aircraft already in service. For new deliveries, Southwest and United have told Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with the affected software and would take aircraft with a previous version instead, CBS reported. The fleet statements cover four U.S. carriers. CBS said it had also contacted Allegiant Air (G4), which operates the 737 MAX, for comment. Boeing told Airways it did not have specific aircraft figures to share, so it remains unclear how many undelivered aircraft carry versions 14 or 14.1, or whether any operator outside the U.S. already flies with them. An airline first told Boeing about the condition in November 2024, according to CBS. Boeing reviewed it and concluded in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue. Boeing received what a source described to CBS as "additional information from operators" earlier this year, which prompted it to launch a formal safety review board. The Wall Street Journal reported that the formal review began in September, according to an Investing.com summary of the newspaper's report . The board's findings went to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by the CARB. Boeing told Airways that it informed the FAA of the issue as part of its safety review process and is working under the agency's oversight to complete the software update. The FAA certified the 737-7 on August 3. CBS reported that the aircraft was certified with software version 14 and that Southwest, which accounts for nearly all of the type's order book, had been set to begin receiving it this fall; it is unclear whether the airline will take delivery now. CNBC reported it was not immediately clear whether the 737-7 could be delivered or flown with an older software version. The 737-10 used version 14.1 during its certification testing, according to CBS. Boeing completed the final planned certification flight in July, and Alaska Chief Operating Officer Jason Berry told Reuters on September 24 that the airline expected FAA certification by the end of September . Aviation Week reported that it remains unclear whether the software issue will affect the timing of either 737-7 deliveries or 737-10 certification. The FAA's statement did not address either program. Alaska said on September 26 that it has been engaged with Boeing and the FAA "and will continue to work closely with both as they evaluate this matter and determine next steps." Alaska holds an order for 105 737-10s and options for 35 more . In his September 24 interview, before the software issue was reported, Berry said Alaska expected its first aircraft in spring 2027 and passenger service between April and mid-May that year. He added that Alaska must complete certification work on the pilots' head-up display after the FAA approves the aircraft, a process he expected to take a "few months." The CARB will review Boeing's safety findings, and the FAA told Airways that the board will also review Boeing's proposed solution. Boeing told Airways it had no further information at this time on whether 737-7 deliveries can proceed with an earlier software load, whether the fix will require pilot training beyond a software update, or what additional operator information prompted its formal safety review. The FAA's statement to Airways did not say whether the CARB must conclude before the agency certifies the 737-10. Copyright © 2026 Airways Publishing LLC. All rights reserved. ‍

sources.title: Alabama launches investigation into OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face - TechCrunch
passages: Alabama’s attorney general announced Monday that it sent a subpoena to OpenAI as part of an investigation into the company’s alleged “complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards” in the Hugging Face incident.

The investigation comes weeks after OpenAI admitted that one of its unreleased and guardrail-free cybersecurity models had escaped an isolated environment, connected to the internet, and hacked AI dataset platform Hugging Face.
The letter also asked OpenAI to “immediately cease and desist” from any internal cybersecurity evaluations.
Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly.”
Lorenzo Franceschi-Bicchierai was a Senior Writer at TechCrunch, where he covered hacking, cybersecurity, surveillance, and privacy.

extraction.body: Alabama’s attorney general announced Monday that it sent a subpoena to OpenAI as part of an investigation into the company’s alleged “complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards” in the Hugging Face incident. The investigation comes weeks after OpenAI admitted that one of its unreleased and guardrail-free cybersecurity models had escaped an isolated environment, connected to the internet, and hacked AI dataset platform Hugging Face. As Reuters first reported , Hugging Face was only one of four victims of what was supposed to be “an internal evaluation” of a model with “maximal cyber capabilities,” as OpenAI put it. The press release announcing the subpoena sent by the state’s attorney general Steve Marshall said that the state was seeking to understand if OpenAI’s “inability or unwillingness to ensure the safety of its products” violated the state’s consumer protection laws. When reached by TechCrunch for comment, OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans provided the statement: “The Hugging Face incident marked an important moment for AI safety and we are conducting a thorough review along with external advisors. Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly.” Earlier this month, Marshall, along with the attorneys general of 14 other states, including Florida, Missouri, Pennsylvania, and Texas, sent a letter to OpenAI’s CEO Sam Altman, requesting that he and his company preserve all records related to the Hugging Face incident. The letter also asked OpenAI to “immediately cease and desist” from any internal cybersecurity evaluations. In the wake of the Hugging Face incident, and several other incidents disclosed by Anthropic, the U.K.’s AI Security Institute, Meta, and workers at AI companies — including executives and technical leaders — signed an open letter called “ Pacing the Frontier ,” which called for developing AI capabilities slowly and more responsibly. The letter also called for the U.S. government to support an “international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” Lorenzo Franceschi-Bicchierai was a Senior Writer at TechCrunch, where he covered hacking, cybersecurity, surveillance, and privacy. sources.title: Nvidia releases AI safety software it says could have stopped Hugging Face hack
passages: Nvidia on Monday made available a set of software safety tools for AI agents that it says would have stopped the hack of Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia paid $13 billion for months after it was swarmed by rogue agents from OpenAI.The move comes as OpenAI and Anthropic, the top two US AI labs, are investigating numerous instances where their agents, which are AI systems capable of carrying out complex tasks, hacked into commercial and government systems.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer.One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents.

Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor.The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might spawn several sub-agents in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia.

extraction.body: Alabama’s attorney general announced Monday that it sent a subpoena to OpenAI as part of an investigation into the company’s alleged “complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards” in the Hugging Face incident. The investigation comes weeks after OpenAI admitted that one of its unreleased and guardrail-free cybersecurity models had escaped an isolated environment, connected to the internet, and hacked AI dataset platform Hugging Face. As Reuters first reported , Hugging Face was only one of four victims of what was supposed to be “an internal evaluation” of a model with “maximal cyber capabilities,” as OpenAI put it. The press release announcing the subpoena sent by the state’s attorney general Steve Marshall said that the state was seeking to understand if OpenAI’s “inability or unwillingness to ensure the safety of its products” violated the state’s consumer protection laws. When reached by TechCrunch for comment, OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans provided the statement: “The Hugging Face incident marked an important moment for AI safety and we are conducting a thorough review along with external advisors. Once the review is complete, we will share a technical report with relevant government authorities and publish our findings publicly.” Earlier this month, Marshall, along with the attorneys general of 14 other states, including Florida, Missouri, Pennsylvania, and Texas, sent a letter to OpenAI’s CEO Sam Altman, requesting that he and his company preserve all records related to the Hugging Face incident. The letter also asked OpenAI to “immediately cease and desist” from any internal cybersecurity evaluations. In the wake of the Hugging Face incident, and several other incidents disclosed by Anthropic, the U.K.’s AI Security Institute, Meta, and workers at AI companies — including executives and technical leaders — signed an open letter called “ Pacing the Frontier ,” which called for developing AI capabilities slowly and more responsibly. The letter also called for the U.S. government to support an “international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” Lorenzo Franceschi-Bicchierai was a Senior Writer at TechCrunch, where he covered hacking, cybersecurity, surveillance, and privacy. sources.title: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving - cnbc.com
passages: Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform to allow AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from breaking out of containment.

The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI , Anthropic , Meta , and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.
"Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company.
"From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks."
One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities.
Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs.
Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market.
"You can't have agents roam around and drift around the company, and so you have to find a way to container it," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday.
Nvidia named Cisco , Microsoft , Oracle , CoreWeave , Dell , HPE , Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners.
Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell.
Huang said the new platform is essentially "a browser for agents," providing a containment system that only allows access to things an agent needs to do its job.

Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers.

But Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development.
An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July.

The Open Agent Safety Platform combines Nvidia’s OpenShell runtime with a new system called Sentry, adding an independent layer that can monitor an agent’s activity and intervene without relying on the model to police itself. Recent incidents have shown why that extra layer may be needed, with agents finding ways around restrictions while completing assigned tasks. Nvidia says the platform could have stopped the Hugging Face incident, where agents escaped a controlled OpenAI testing environment and reached systems they were never supposed to access. Nvidia’s approach puts some enforcement outside the model itself, giving technology organizations another layer of control when model-level safeguards fall short. As agents move into production, that separation could become an important part of determining how much access they can safely be trusted with. Huang said the new platform is essentially "a browser for agents," providing a containment system that only allows access to things an agent needs to do its job. The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI , Anthropic , Meta , and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems. An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July. That's when OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached Hugging Face, which operates an open-source developer platform. "Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company. "From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks." Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers. But Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development. "You have to think about what you could have done, what's the solution for it," Huang said in a podcast with The New York Times' Ezra Klein released last week, referring to recent incidents. "In the future, improve your process so that you could avoid this from happening again." Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei set off an industry firestorm two weeks ago, urging AI model developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of the models spinning out of control, an argument that was supported by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk . Nvidia's new offering is an engineering solution to the agent safety issue, Boitano said. "Recent incidents have highlighted a fundamental hurdle for AI agents, and that is that model-level safeguards alone can't govern what agents can access or do," Boitano said. One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities. Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs. Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market. Nvidia named Cisco , Microsoft , Oracle , CoreWeave , Dell , HPE , Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners. Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell. "We can't have a successful AI industry if the world doesn't think it's built or confident that it's built and deployed safely," Huang told CNBC on Monday. Got a confidential news tip? extraction.body: Nvidia is rolling out a new security system designed to keep AI agents contained when they start acting outside the boundaries set for them. The Open Agent Safety Platform combines Nvidia’s OpenShell runtime with a new system called Sentry, adding an independent layer that can monitor an agent’s activity and intervene without relying on the model to police itself. Recent incidents have shown why that extra layer may be needed, with agents finding ways around restrictions while completing assigned tasks. Nvidia says the platform could have stopped the Hugging Face incident, where agents escaped a controlled OpenAI testing environment and reached systems they were never supposed to access. Why It Matters: Recent incidents have shown AI agents bypassing restrictions to complete their tasks, raising questions about how companies can keep them within approved boundaries. Nvidia’s approach puts some enforcement outside the model itself, giving technology organizations another layer of control when model-level safeguards fall short. As agents move into production, that separation could become an important part of determining how much access they can safely be trusted with. FILE - A logo of Nvidia is displayed at at the Computex Taipei exhibition, one of the world's largest computer and technology expos, in Taipei, Taiwan, Wednesday, June 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Chiang Ying-ying, File) Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform designed to stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue , saying it sets “boundaries” that could have stopped previous breaches. The announcement of the company's Open Agent Safety Platform follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations. The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control. Nvidia executives said in a media briefing the new, open-source system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face . “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI. The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed the safety concerns about AI, which was followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI's models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own. Earlence Fernandes, an associate professor at the University of California, San Diego's computer science and engineering department, called Nvidia's security platform a “step in the right direction.” “We need more work that seeks to build protections around the model. I’ve been talking about how traditional cybersecurity ideas are necessary to help control and secure AI agents for a while now," he said in an email. “There are however, several challenges that traditional cyber security approaches still cannot currently solve. For example, what is a good security policy to configure the system with? An agent needs access to real resources to be useful, but giving it the minimum amount of access is tricky and non-trivial.” Fernandes added that to solve the AI security problem, both sides need to cooperate, with companies continuing to invest in alignment efforts and the open source community and academia "creating systems-level solutions to account for when a model does engage in unwanted behavior.” Nvidia, based in Santa Clara, California, makes high-end chips that have emerged as the leading building blocks for AI. The company's board has cleared the way for the company to spend $150 billion more in share buybacks , bringing its stock repurchase program to $235 billion, the company said Monday. Nvidia's security software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said. Because it's open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel. The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard chips to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can "intervene instantly" if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said. “OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” he said. Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase. The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. But others including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address. Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform designed to stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue , saying it sets “boundaries” that could have stopped previous breaches.
The announcement of the company's Open Agent Safety Platform follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations.
The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control.

Nvidia executives said in a media briefing the new, open-source system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face .

“From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI.

The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed the safety concerns about AI, which was followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI's models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own.
Earlence Fernandes, an associate professor at the University of California, San Diego's computer science and engineering department, called Nvidia's security platform a “step in the right direction.”

“We need more work that seeks to build protections around the model. I’ve been talking about how traditional cybersecurity ideas are necessary to help control and secure AI agents for a while now," he said in an email. “There are however, several challenges that traditional cyber security approaches still cannot currently solve. For example, what is a good security policy to configure the system with? An agent needs access to real resources to be useful, but giving it the minimum amount of access is tricky and non-trivial.”

Fernandes added that to solve the AI security problem, both sides need to cooperate, with companies continuing to invest in alignment efforts and the open source community and academia "creating systems-level solutions to account for when a model does engage in unwanted behavior.”

Nvidia, based in Santa Clara, California, makes high-end chips that have emerged as the leading building blocks for AI. The company's board has cleared the way for the company to spend $150 billion more in share buybacks , bringing its stock repurchase program to $235 billion, the company said Monday.
Nvidia's security software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said.
Because it's open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel.

The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard chips to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can "intervene instantly" if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said.
“It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said.
“OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” he said.
Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase.

The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. But others including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release.

Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.

The company said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that “sets boundaries for agents,” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations. The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control. Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face . “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI. The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed the safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI's models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own. Nvidia's software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said. Because it's open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel. The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can "intervene instantly" if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said. “OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” Boitano said. Nvidia said more than 100 organizations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture, and JPMorgan Chase. sources.title: Chainlink connects banks to Swift blockchain ledger
passages: Chainlink will connect bank systems and signing infrastructure to Swift’s blockchain ledger through its platform.
Chainlink did not provide a timetable for individual banks to adopt its connection framework or identify which of Swift’s pilot banks will use CRE first.
Sergey Nazarov, CEO of Chainlink Labs, said the company was “thrilled to be supporting the Swift ledger” as banks seek technology for tokenized deposits and ledger connectivity.
The latest work extends a relationship between Chainlink and Swift that has covered institutional blockchain interoperability for several years.
Swift has stressed that the blockchain ledger does not replace its role as a global financial messaging network.
As crypto.news previously reported, Swift’s first ledger deployment uses tokenized deposits issued by banks instead of a public cryptocurrency bridge asset.
Swift’s ledger supports 24/7 tokenized deposit payments while final settlement continues through existing agreed mechanisms.
Swift says its network connects more than 11,500 institutions and corporates across over 200 markets.
Swift disclosed in March that the ledger’s first iteration uses an Ethereum Virtual Machine-compatible architecture based on Hyperledger Besu, an open-source enterprise blockchain platform.
Swift operates the ledger and coordinates interbank processes, including validation of funding commitments.
CRE lets institutions retain transaction signing keys while orchestrating workflows that access Swift’s shared ledger.
The deposits remain on bank-owned ledgers, while Swift coordinates payment commitments between participating institutions before final settlement.

Previous work examined how financial institutions could use existing Swift infrastructure alongside blockchain networks, including experiments involving tokenized assets and cross-chain communication.
Swift itself remains the operator of the new ledger.
Chainlink describes CRE as the workflow layer responsible for coordinating interactions while each bank signs its own transactions.
Chainlink repeated the same distinction in its Sept.

Announced Sept. 28, the project will use the Chainlink Runtime Environment, or CRE, service to connect current institutional platforms with services on a shared ledger built by Swift.
The architecture includes secure self-signing. Banks retain their transaction-signing keys, and CRE provides an intermediary layer for bank access to the ledger.
According to Chainlink, financial institutions can use a tokenized payment system without relinquishing signing control to a third party or compromising other controls over their operations.

The framework would help with the use of smart contracts between banks and on the Swift blockchain. Tokenized deposits would still be bank liabilities held on bank blockchains.

Swift’s common infrastructure can help settle and verify payment obligations between participants. Other settlement methods, such as real-time gross settlement systems and correspondent relationships, can be used for the final settlement of payments.

The partnership builds on previous collaborations between Chainlink and Swift to promote blockchain interoperability within the institutional sector. Chainlink and UBS worked together in 2025 to implement blockchain and CRE digital asset processes using Swift communications.

Swift’s proposed ledger is designed to facilitate around-the-clock international commercial bank payments using tokenized commercial bank deposits, not a public cryptocurrency as an intermediary asset.

Chainlink did not provide a timetable for individual banks to adopt its connection framework or identify which of Swift’s pilot banks will use CRE first.

Now, the CSU is again inviting input from its community, explicitly seeking perspectives from those through a new survey open until October 19. Professor and Chair of the Academic Senate Jackson Wilson is using data from last year’s responses to pinpoint whether attitudes and behaviors around AI are shifting, directly informing future policy decisions. “AI is changing quickly, and campuses need to understand how our students, faculty and staff are actually experiencing it,” said Andrew Roderick, SFSU assistant vice president of Academic Technology. The California State University is actively quantifying shifts in attitudes toward artificial intelligence, with the current survey specifically designed to identify whether concerns and behaviors observed last year are holding steady or evolving. This follow-up study aims to provide a longitudinal understanding of AI adoption and apprehension, directly informing future policy decisions across the 23-campus system. The scope of the current inquiry extends beyond those actively using AI. The CSU explicitly invites input from individuals to gain a comprehensive picture of sentiment. You don’t have to like AI. We want to hear from everyone.” This inclusive strategy acknowledges that understanding resistance to the technology is as important as understanding its adoption. Participants completing the anonymous, ten-minute survey can also enter a drawing for a $25 gift card or an iPad, incentivizing broad participation through October 19. Initial findings from last year’s survey revealed widespread concerns regarding AI’s accuracy, potential impacts on academic integrity and ethical considerations, alongside anxieties about job security and the need for enhanced training resources. Wilson elaborated on the nuances of those earlier responses, explaining, “The previous study indicated that overall students have multiple concerns with AI; however, there are differences between groups of students in how that angst is impacting their behavior.” Understanding whether these varied anxieties persist, intensify, or diminish over time is central to the CSU’s ongoing evaluation of AI integration. sources.title: Nvidia releases AI safety software it says could have stopped Hugging Face hack - AOL.com
passages: SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Nvidia on Monday made available a set of software safety tools for AI agents that it says would have stopped the hack of Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia paid $13 billion for months after it was swarmed by rogue agents from OpenAI.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer.

The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia.
One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents.
Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system also works on their central processors.
Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor.
Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, including Anthropic.

The move comes as OpenAI and Anthropic, the top two US AI labs, are investigating numerous instances where their agents, which are AI systems capable of carrying out complex tasks, hacked into commercial and government systems. Justin Boitano, vice president and general manager of enterprise computing at Nvidia, said the tools would have stopped the Hugging Face attack disclosed this summer. “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” Boitano said during a media briefing. “We’re advancing this openly, and we want to engage everybody to work with us.” Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor. "This is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," Golshan said during a briefing. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; editing by Lincoln Feast.)

passages: Nvidia , a top chipmaker whose products fuel many artificial intelligence agents, released a software platform on Monday designed to prevent security incidents revealed by AI firms in recent months.
"Recent security incidents have underscored the need to equip organizations with open, customizable tools that enforce more control over long-running agents," Nvidia said in a statement .
The move comes after a flurry of AI security incidents disclosed by firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet-owned Google.

coreStoryFacts.text: SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Nvidia on Monday made available a set of software safety tools for AI agents that it says would have stopped the hack of Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia paid $13 billion for months after it was swarmed by rogue agents from OpenAI.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer.

The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia.
One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents.
Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system also works on their central processors.
Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor.
Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, including Anthropic.

The move comes as OpenAI and Anthropic, the top two US AI labs, are investigating numerous instances where their agents, which are AI systems capable of carrying out complex tasks, hacked into commercial and government systems. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer. One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents. Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system also works on their central processors. Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, including Anthropic. Justin Boitano, vice president and general manager of enterprise computing at Nvidia, said the tools would have stopped the Hugging Face attack disclosed this summer. “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” Boitano said during a media briefing. “We’re advancing this openly, and we want to engage everybody to work with us.” Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor. The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia. "This is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," Golshan said during a briefing. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; editing by Lincoln Feast.)

sources.title: Nvidia releases AI safety software it says could have stopped Hugging Face hack - AOL.com
passages: SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Nvidia on Monday made available a set of software safety tools for AI agents that it says would have stopped the hack of Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia paid $13 billion for months after it was swarmed by rogue agents from OpenAI.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer.

The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia.
One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents.
Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system also works on their central processors.
Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor.
Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, including Anthropic.

extraction.body: SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Nvidia on Monday made available a set of software safety tools for AI agents that it says would have stopped the hack of Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia paid $13 billion for months after it was swarmed by rogue agents from OpenAI. The move comes as OpenAI and Anthropic, the top two US AI labs, are investigating numerous instances where their agents, which are AI systems capable of carrying out complex tasks, hacked into commercial and government systems. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer. One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents. Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system also works on their central processors. Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, including Anthropic. Justin Boitano, vice president and general manager of enterprise computing at Nvidia, said the tools would have stopped the Hugging Face attack disclosed this summer. “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” Boitano said during a media briefing. “We’re advancing this openly, and we want to engage everybody to work with us.” Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor. The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia. "This is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," Golshan said during a briefing. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; editing by Lincoln Feast.)

extraction.body: SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Nvidia on Monday made available a set of software safety tools for AI agents that it says would have stopped the hack of Hugging Face, the AI coding hub that Nvidia paid $13 billion for months after it was swarmed by rogue agents from OpenAI. The move comes as OpenAI and Anthropic, the top two US AI labs, are investigating numerous instances where their agents, which are AI systems capable of carrying out complex tasks, hacked into commercial and government systems. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, head of the world's largest company whose chips have powered most of the AI boom, has rejected calls for broad AI safety regulations and instead framed the escaped agents as an engineering problem to be solved, akin to making automobiles safer. One tool released Monday called OpenShell uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents. Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system also works on their central processors. Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, including Anthropic. Justin Boitano, vice president and general manager of enterprise computing at Nvidia, said the tools would have stopped the Hugging Face attack disclosed this summer. “From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” Boitano said during a media briefing. “We’re advancing this openly, and we want to engage everybody to work with us.” Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip in tandem with OpenShell to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor. The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia. "This is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," Golshan said during a briefing. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; editing by Lincoln Feast.)
