extraction.body: Officials say the prototype software will have lower accuracy levels, but faster observations and analysis for space surveillance. The U.S. Space Force is going even more high-tech by developing new software that will combine commercial and military flight tracking data into one component to deliver more timely and accurate information. Col. Barry Croker, who heads up the Space Force’s Mission Delta 2 , and spoke at this month's annual Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance (AMOSS) conference in Hawaii, said the plan is to launch the prototype software later this fall and build a “viable product” that can be up and running quickly. "Space control begins with space domain awareness, as we cannot protect or defend what we do not track," Col. Crocker said in a statement to Military.com. "Mission Delta 2 is prototyping new software to meet warfighter timelines by establishing a combat-oriented tactical catalog that prioritizes decision velocity and operational custody over legacy catalog perfection." Mission Delta 2 is responsible for organizing, training and equipping Space Force operations. It includes the 18th and 19th Space Defense Squadrons that operate the Space Surveillance Network of telescopes and radars around the globe and the software systems required to analyze the data they gather about space objects, in particular those operated by potential adversaries. "The standards required for civil spaceflight safety should not limit tactical action. By shifting our data integration architecture, our prototype rapidly absorbs, correlates, and operationalizes commercial data that was previously excluded by legacy fidelity thresholds," Col. Crocker added. " Our intent is to leverage sensors we already possess and network them to deliver faster combat support to the Joint Force.” According to Crocker, current military software and processes for analyzing data are biased toward accuracy rather than timeliness. By contrast, he said the prototype software will have lower accuracy levels, but faster observations and analysis. “I now have the opportunity to get a more timely state of something, even if it’s not perfect,” Crocker told a gathering of reporters at the AMOSS conference. “Now I can start to have a more timely indication of what’s going on. So that’s big. That’s the number one focus." The new prototype software launch was a hot topic at the AMOSS conference, where scientists converged to discuss the latest advances in space exploration, optics and surveillance. Conference leaders estimate 500,000 pieces of space junk are circling the Earth. "Space has become so very, very busy. It's full of debris. It's full of flying spacecraft," Elliot Pullham, CEO of Space Foundation, said in a conference video viewed by Military.com. "It's just a very treacherous environment to operate in, and the capability for understanding that and managing that resides here on Maui. And so it's important for us all to get together and talk about that." Hawaii is widely considered to have some of the best high-altitude observatory sites in the world, with researchers at the University of Hawaii at the forefront. In 2023, an observatory site at the Maui Space Surveillance Complex located atop the 10,000-foot summit of the Haleakalā volcano broke, causing a 700-gallon fuel spill that made headlines. "So to be able to contribute to the world by providing these sites, sharing these sites, so that we can monitor and catalog the objects that we have in space, as well as the heavens beyond, is just extremely fortunate for the University of Hawaii," Mike Maberry, assistant director at the University of Hawaii's Institute for Astronomy, said in the AMOSS conference video. Until the new software is operational, Crocker said the Space Force will continue to use commercial space tracking information via the Joint Commercial Operations cell. The data is housed in the cloud-based Unified Data Library, but it is not shared directly into military computer tracking systems. The goal is to ensure precise targeting of adversary satellites and to be able to automatically integrate commercial space tracking data. “We could take the largest step forward if we could just better integrate the commercial data and consistently fund the acquisition of that data, and then be able to drive it into our programs of record for space domain awareness," Gen. Stephen Whiting, commander of SPACECOM, told the publication "Breaking Defense" at the AMOSS conference. "That would be the biggest initial step we could take, and we could take that in the short term." extraction.body: Amid the growing concerns over aviation safety, reports are emerging that Boeing has identified a software glitch in the 737 Max that could cause the automated navigation feature to fail, prompting a major safety risk while the planes are landing. The revalation was made in a Wall Street Journal report. While Boeing acknowledged the risk, it hasn't made a public disclosure on the matter as of now. As per the report, the glitch emerged from a cockpit software update and can occur when flight crews alter their planned flight path following a missed approach. However, experts warned that by flying manually in such circumstances, a pilot could overlook something while they are already busy, at low altitude, and possibly dealing with situations like bad weather. As per the report, the aerospace giant, airlines and regulators have been assessing the glitch and whether it poses a flight safety issue. It is pertinent to note that Boeing notified the 737 Max operators about the glitch in late August. At that time, they argued that it didn't pose a safety risk, according to the company document viewed by The Wall Street Journal. In the memo, the company said that it was working with airlines on a procedure to allow pilots to re-enable the automated navigation feature if needed, and was also devising a software fix. “We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases,” Boeing said. “Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue.” Airline carrier remains concerned Amid the news of the glitch, Southwest Airlines and United Airlines have told Boeing that they don’t want to receive new 737 MAX planes equipped with the flawed software. Meanwhile, a senior official of the Federal Aviation Administration said that the agency will take action if needed. The matter has been concerning since the American plane maker has had a checkered safety record, and it has been working to restore trust with regulators, airline customers and the flying public. The accidents led to intense scrutiny that delayed FAA approvals for newer versions of the jet. It is still unknown how many 737 MAX jets might be flying with the flawed software. The software issue could complicate airlines’ plans to fly Boeing’s newest 737 models, the MAX 7 and MAX 10, government and industry officials told WSJ. The FAA approved the MAX 7 for passenger service last month with the new software, the senior agency official said. Boeing Chief Executive Kelly Ortberg has said recently that he expects regulators to soon approve the MAX 10.
